title: DRX Kits
description:
DRX is CRL's patented modular door rail. Glass temperers and glaziers stock the components and cut rails to length in their own shop instead of waiting on a factory-built custom rail. But it was only sold in packs of ten, which made the first purchase hard to justify. DRX Kits put everything for one rail in a single box, so an installer can try the system on one door.

We repurposed existing DRX inventory into 16 kit SKUs (square and tapered profiles, four finishes, with and without locks), positioned pricing against the custom rails buyers already ordered, and took the kits through five gates in six months with engineering, marketing, sales, planning and production.

metrics.label: Kit SKUs built from existing inventory

brief.label: Problem
brief.text: DRX had been on the market for two and a half years, but buyers had to purchase at least ten of every component to finish a single door.

brief.label: Customers
brief.text: Glass temperers, large and small glazing contractors and door repair shops, working on commercial offices, government buildings, retail and hospitality.

brief.label: Solution
brief.text: A complete single-rail kit: two rail bodies, a slide block, two 48" side covers, gasket and end caps. The covers are cut from existing 110" stock, so kits ship immediately with no manufacturing lead time.

brief.label: Value
brief.text: Installers get a modular, adjustable system that installs faster. Temperers stop waiting on factory fabrication. Owners can change finishes after installation.

brief.label: Market
brief.text: Glass office market of $500–600M (2021), forecast to grow 7–8% a year through 2028.

swot.strengths:
Everything for one door rail in one box, so ordering and installing is simpler
Installers' inventory gets easier to manage
swot.weaknesses:
DRX costs more than the standard DRS rail
Internal teams needed training and buy-in on a newer system
swot.opportunities:
Reach buyers frustrated with custom-rail lead times
Give glaziers and temperers control over their own schedules
Build loyalty with customers who adopt the system
swot.threats:
Competitors could copy the kit approach
For some buyers the cost may outweigh the benefit

my_role: I co-led DRX Kits with the senior product manager and ran it through all five gates in six months. I built the business case from custom-rail sales, defined the 16 SKUs and their pricing and discount rules, wrote the inventory plan, and coordinated manufacturing to repackage existing stock into kits instead of tooling anything new.

recovery_title: Plan to win back DRX sales
recovery_intro: DRX launched to a strong forecast, but first-year sales reached about a third of plan and the second year fell further behind. Buyers liked the system; the ten-pack minimum stopped them from trying it.

recovery.label: Remove the minimum
recovery.text: Sell everything for one door rail in a single box, so the first purchase is one door, not ten.

recovery.label: Use what's on the shelf
recovery.text: Kits were built from existing DRX inventory at the service centers and plant, turning slow stock into sellable product with no new tooling.

recovery.label: Price against the real alternative
recovery.text: Kits were priced against the custom factory rails buyers were already ordering, with a target of converting 10% of custom-rail demand in the first year.

recovery.label: Build the habit, then the stock
recovery.text: Glaziers try DRX on one door; as demand builds, temperers have a reason to stock full packs again.

challenges.challenge: Early part numbering reused one number for blank, lock-prepared and panic-prepared rails, which would have broken ordering and costing.
challenges.resolution: We dropped the panic option for launch, gave every variant a unique number following CRL's existing lock-suffix logic, and launched with nut strips customers can swap for other glass thicknesses instead of multiplying SKUs.

challenges.challenge: The kits had to be cheaper to build than the custom rail they replaced, using parts that were already made.
challenges.resolution: Engineering ran a cost comparison of DRX against the equivalent custom rail before we committed; the kit came in lower, which set our pricing floor.
